issue.issue_text: Whether conviction of appellant-accused no.6 justified.

facts: The appellant, accused no. 6, was convicted for being part of a large mob that committed several offences.
His conviction was based entirely on the testimony of a single witness, PW-2.
PW-2 identified the appellant for the first time in court, approximately two years after the incident, as the person who snatched her gold chain.
The witness (PW-2) did not know the appellant before the incident.
The appellant was part of a large, aggressive mob of 50 to 100 people.
No identification parade was held to identify the appellant prior to the in-court identification.
law: A conviction based on the testimony of a solitary witness is unsafe if that witness's evidence is not considered 'wholly reliable'.
If a witness's evidence is categorized as 'neither wholly reliable nor wholly unreliable', a conviction can only be sustained if there is corroboration from other direct or circumstantial evidence.
application: The Court found the testimony of the sole witness, PW-2, to be unreliable.

The identification of the appellant was considered doubtful for several reasons: it occurred for the first time in court after a two-year delay, the appellant was a stranger to the witness, he was part of a large and chaotic mob, and no prior identification parade was conducted.
The Court reasoned that due to the chaotic circumstances, PW-2 would not have had adequate time or opportunity to note the appellant's distinctive features.
The Court found that there was a complete absence of any direct or circumstantial evidence to corroborate PW-2's testimony.
Therefore, relying solely on PW-2's doubtful identification to prove guilt beyond a reasonable doubt was deemed unsafe.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the conviction of the appellant could not be sustained because it was based on the uncorroborated and unreliable testimony of a single witness whose identification of the appellant was doubtful. Consequently, the Court accepted the appeal and acquitted the appellant.

issue.issue_text: Whether conviction of accused no. 2, 3, 4 was justified, when role ascribed to them was that they were part of mob.

facts: Accused nos. 2, 3, and 4 were convicted based on the allegation that they were part of a mob.
No specific overt acts were attributed to them.
Their conviction relied on the identification testimony of two witnesses, PW-25 and PW-26.
In a previous appeal involving other co-accused from the same case (nos. 1, 5, and 13), a coordinate bench of the Supreme Court had already acquitted them.
law: The Court applied the principle of parity, which suggests that individuals who are similarly situated should receive similar treatment.
The Court relied on the precedent set by its own coordinate bench in the same case, which had already evaluated and made a finding on the credibility of the key witnesses.
application: The Supreme Court noted that the conviction of accused nos. 1, 5, and 13 had been based solely on the testimony of witnesses PW-25 and PW-26.
In the earlier decision, the Court had discarded the testimony of these two witnesses in its entirety, finding it to be unreliable.

The Court reasoned that since accused nos. 2, 3, and 4 were in a similar position, with their convictions also resting on the testimony of the same unreliable witnesses, the benefit of the earlier finding must be extended to them.
It was also noted that no other witnesses had ascribed any role to accused nos. 2, 3, and 4.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the conviction of accused nos. 2, 3, and 4 was not justified. Because the only evidence against them came from witnesses whose testimony had already been deemed entirely unreliable by the Court in the same case, their conviction was set aside.

issue.issue_text: Whether the jurisdiction under Article 136 of the Constitution of India can be invoked in favour of a non-appealing party even suo moto.

facts: Accused nos. 1, 5, and 13 were acquitted by the Supreme Court after the testimony used to convict them was rejected as unreliable.
Accused nos. 3 and 4 were convicted based on the same evidence but had not filed an appeal to the Supreme Court.
The Court found that the case against accused nos. 3 and 4 stood on the exact same footing as the case against the acquitted accused.
law: The Supreme Court has jurisdiction under Article 136 of the Constitution to act in favor of a party even if they have not appealed (suo moto).
This suo moto power is to be used very sparingly, with caution, and only in the 'rarest of the rare cases' where a compelling ground exists.
Failing to extend the same relief to individuals in identical situations (parity) can amount to a violation of their fundamental right to liberty under Article 21 of the Constitution.
application: The Court applied the principle of parity, stating that since accused nos. 3 and 4 were in the same position as the acquitted accused, they must receive the same benefit.
It reasoned that allowing the conviction of accused nos. 3 and 4 to stand would violate their fundamental rights under Article 21.
This potential violation of liberty was considered a compelling ground, justifying the rare and cautious use of its suo moto powers under Article 136.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that it can invoke its jurisdiction under Article 136 suo moto in favor of a non-appealing party. It did so in this case to extend the benefit of acquittal to accused nos. 3 and 4 to maintain parity with other acquitted accused and to prevent a violation of their fundamental right to liberty.

issue.issue_text: Whether an order refusing special leave to appeal by a non-speaking order attracts the doctrine of merger, thereby preventing the Court from recalling it to grant relief on the basis of parity.

facts: A special leave petition previously filed by an accused (accused no. 2) had been summarily dismissed by the Supreme Court without any reasons being recorded (a non-speaking order).
Subsequently, other co-accused (nos. 1, 5, and 13), whose cases were based on similar evidence and stood on the same footing, were acquitted by the Court.
This created a situation where accused no. 2 remained convicted while similarly situated co-accused were acquitted, raising the question of parity.
law: The doctrine of merger does not apply when a special leave petition is refused by a non-speaking order. This is a well-settled principle of law.

The principle of parity dictates that when there is similar or identical evidence against multiple accused with similar roles, a court cannot convict one while acquitting another. Like cases must be decided alike to avoid discrimination.
Failing to grant relief on the basis of parity can amount to a manifest injustice and a violation of the accused's fundamental rights under Article 21 of the Constitution of India.
application: The Court first established that because the earlier dismissal of accused no. 2's petition was a non-speaking order, the doctrine of merger was not attracted. This meant the Court was not prevented from reconsidering its own order.
The Court then found that the case of accused no. 2 was identical to that of the co-accused who had been acquitted.
Applying the principle of parity, the Court reasoned that accused no. 2 must be given the same benefit as the acquitted co-accused.
The Court concluded that allowing the conviction to stand would be a manifest injustice and a violation of accused no. 2's constitutional rights.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument that the doctrine of merger applied. It held that a non-speaking order dismissing a special leave petition does not prevent the Court from later recalling that order to grant relief on the grounds of parity. Therefore, the Court recalled its earlier order to ensure that accused no. 2 received the same benefit of acquittal as the other similarly situated accused.

arguments.issue_text: Whether conviction of appellant-accused no.6 justified.
appellant_arguments: The overall case of the prosecution is weak, as demonstrated by the fact that the testimony of key witnesses (PW-25 and PW-26), which was the basis for convicting other co-accused, was completely discarded by the Supreme Court in a related appeal.
respondent_arguments: PW-2 clearly identified the appellant and ascribed the role of snatching her gold chain to him.
The two-year gap between the incident and the deposition was not too long for PW-2 to identify the appellant.
As a woman whose gold chain was snatched, PW-2 would never forget the face of the accused.

arguments.issue_text: Whether conviction of accused no. 2, 3, 4 was justified, when role ascribed to them was that they were part of mob.
appellant_arguments: Accused nos. 2, 3, and 4 were convicted solely on the basis of testimony from PW-25 and PW-26.
The Supreme Court, in a previous appeal for co-accused (nos. 1, 5, and 13), had completely discarded the testimony of these same two witnesses.
Therefore, the benefit of acquittal should be extended to accused nos. 2, 3, and 4 on the grounds of parity.
respondent_arguments: The conviction of accused nos. 2, 3, and 4 has become final and cannot be interfered with.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the jurisdiction under Article 136 of the Constitution of India can be invoked in favour of a non-appealing party even suo moto.
appellant_arguments: The court should exercise its jurisdiction to extend the benefit of the judgment to accused nos. 2, 3, and 4, even though they did not appeal, to ensure justice and maintain parity with acquitted co-accused.
respondent_arguments: The conviction of the non-appealing accused has become final and the court should not interfere.

arguments.issue_text: Whether an order refusing special leave to appeal by a non-speaking order attracts the doctrine of merger, thereby preventing the Court from recalling it to grant relief on the basis of parity.
appellant_arguments: The summary dismissal of the SLP filed by accused no. 2 does not prevent the court from granting him relief on the basis of parity with other acquitted co-accused.
respondent_arguments: The conviction of accused no. 2 has become final because his SLP was summarily dismissed, and the matter cannot be interfered with.

cases.case_name: Musa Khan & Ors. v. State of Maharashtra
cases.principle: The jurisdiction under Article 136 of the Constitution can be invoked in favour of a party even suo moto when the Court is satisfied that compelling grounds exist, but this power should be used very sparingly, with caution, and only in the rarest of rare cases.

cases.case_name: Pawan Kumar v. State of Haryana
cases.principle: The jurisdiction under Article 136 of the Constitution of India can be invoked in favour of a party even suo moto when the Court is satisfied that a compelling ground for its exercise exists.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: When there is similar or identical evidence of eyewitnesses against multiple accused by ascribing them the same or similar role, a court cannot convict one accused and acquit another, as the cases are governed by the principle of parity. The Supreme Court can invoke its jurisdiction under Article 136 of the Constitution of India suo moto to extend the benefit of acquittal to a non-appealing co-accused to prevent a miscarriage of justice, though this power must be exercised sparingly and with caution.
obiter: Whether corroboration of the testimony of a single witness is or is not necessary, must depend upon the facts and circumstances of each case, and no general rule can be laid down.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: When the conviction of co-accused is based solely on evidence that this Court has already discarded as unreliable in a previous appeal for other co-accused, the principle of parity must be applied. Failing to extend the benefit of acquittal to the remaining co-accused, even those who did not appeal or whose special leave petition was summarily dismissed, would constitute a violation of their fundamental rights under Article 21 of the Constitution and amount to manifest injustice.
legal_tests_applied: The jurisdiction under Article 136 of the Constitution of India can be invoked in favour of a non-appealing party even suo moto when the Court is satisfied that a compelling ground for its exercise exists, though this power must be used very sparingly and in the rarest of rare cases.

The principle of parity requires that if accused persons stand on the same footing, and the evidence against them is identical to that which was rejected for acquitted co-accused, they must also be granted the benefit of acquittal.

The summary dismissal of a special leave petition by a non-speaking order does not attract the doctrine of merger and does not prevent the Court from recalling the order to prevent a manifest injustice and grant relief on the basis of parity.
policy_considerations: If the same relief is not extended to accused nos. 3 and 4 by reason of parity, it will amount to violation of fundamental rights guaranteed to accused nos. 3 and 4 by Article 21 of the Constitution of India.
The suo motu exercise of powers under Article 136 is warranted as it is a question of the liberty of the said two accused guaranteed by Article 21 of the Constitution.
If we fail to grant relief to accused no 2, the rights guaranteed to accused no. 2 under Article 21 of the Constitution of India will be violated. It will amount to doing manifest injustice.
As a Constitutional Court entrusted with the duty of upholding fundamental rights guaranteed under the Constitution, it is our duty and obligation to extend the same relief to accused no.2.
